title: Tools of the Storyteller
objectives: I can use ten story words to talk about who tells a story and how it is built.
I can name a character's traits and attitude and prove them with actions.
I can use the prefixes re- and dis- and the ending -ful to understand words.
I can write about a story using exact words such as conflict and resolution.
rationale: A literary unit gives students the vocabulary for explaining why characters act as they do and how a story builds from conflict to resolution. The ten words sort into the shape of a plot (conflict, suspense, flashback, resolution), the people in the story (narrator, trait, attitude, reaction), and effort and secrets (struggle, disclose). It builds on the trait words from unit 1 (ambitious, selfish) and the cause-and-effect phrase as a result from unit 2. The passage is a dialogue between a teacher and two students about an invented story, so each word is used the way readers actually use it in a book discussion.

words.def: A part of a story that goes back to an earlier time.
words.ex: A flashback in the movie showed the hero as a small child.
words.ex2: The writer used a flashback to explain why Rosa was afraid of dogs.
words.nonExample: A scene that jumps ahead to the next day is not a flashback.

apps.academic: A flashback gives background that helps readers understand what a character does.
apps.spoken: There was a flashback to when she was little.
apps.writing: Use flashback for a scene that takes the reader back in time.

cloze.s: The story paused for a ___ that showed Grandpa playing soccer when he was ten years old.

cloze2.s: A ___ in the chapter took us back to the day the family first moved to the city.

misuse.s: The flashback showed what would happen in the future, a year after the story ended.
misuse.why: A flashback goes back to an earlier time; it does not jump forward.

visual.alt: A rewind arrow beside an open book.

words.def: A problem that a character must face in a story.
words.ex: The main conflict in the story is between the wolf and the three pigs.
words.ex2: The conflict in the book begins when Mia's best friend moves away.
words.nonExample: A story where nothing ever goes wrong has no conflict.

apps.academic: Every plot has a conflict that drives the characters to act.
apps.spoken: The conflict is that she wants to go, but he wants to stay.
apps.writing: Use conflict to name the main problem in a story.

cloze.s: The ___ in the story begins when two brothers both claim the same treasure map.

cloze2.s: A character's ___ with a storm made the sailors fear for their lives.

misuse.s: The story had no conflict because the characters faced a terrible problem on every page.
misuse.why: A conflict is a problem the characters face; a story full of problems has one.

visual.alt: A book with a burst beside it showing a problem.

words.frame: The conflict in the story is ___.

words.def: The voice or character that tells a story.
words.ex: The narrator of the story is a young girl who tells it in her own words.
words.ex2: In many folktales, the narrator is a storyteller outside the action.
words.nonExample: A character who only speaks in dialogue is not the narrator.

apps.academic: A first-person narrator uses the word I and tells only what that character knows.
apps.spoken: Who is the narrator in this chapter?
apps.writing: Use narrator for the voice that tells the story.

cloze.s: Because the ___ was Mia herself, we only knew what she saw and felt in the story.

cloze2.s: A calm ___ described the storm from far away without ever using the word I.

misuse.s: The narrator is a character who never tells any part of the story.
misuse.why: The narrator is the voice that tells the story, so a narrator who tells nothing makes no sense.

visual.alt: A microphone beside an open book.

words.frame: The narrator tells the story from ___.

words.def: A quality that shows what a person or character is like.
words.ex: Kindness is Leo's best trait; he helps everyone he meets.
words.ex2: The author shows the character's brave trait when he climbs the tower.
words.nonExample: The color of a character's shirt is not a trait.

apps.academic: Readers learn a character's traits from what the character says and does.
apps.writing: Use trait for a quality, such as brave or kind, that a character shows.

cloze.s: Honesty is her best ___; she always tells the truth, even when it is hard.

cloze2.s: Readers learn about a character's ___ by watching what he or she does.

misuse.s: A trait is the color of the book's cover.
misuse.why: A trait is a quality of a person or character, not a part of a book.

visual.alt: A smiling face made of puzzle pieces.

words.def: The excited, nervous feeling of waiting to find out what happens.
words.ex: The music created suspense as the hero crept toward the dark door.
words.ex2: Readers felt suspense when the clock ticked down and the key was still missing.
words.nonExample: A story that explains everything at once has no suspense.

apps.academic: Authors build suspense by making readers wonder what will happen next.
apps.spoken: The suspense was so strong I could not stop reading.
apps.writing: Use suspense for the feeling of not knowing what comes next.

cloze.s: The creaking floorboards added ___ as we waited to see who was at the door.

cloze2.s: She kept reading because the ___ was so strong that she had to know how it ended.

misuse.s: The scene was full of suspense because everyone already knew exactly what would happen and felt calm.
misuse.why: Suspense comes from not knowing what will happen; knowing everything removes it.

visual.alt: A worried face looking at an open book.

words.def: How someone feels or acts because of something that happens.
words.ex: His reaction to the surprise party was a huge smile.
words.ex2: The dog's reaction to the thunder was to hide under the bed.
words.nonExample: A plan made weeks ahead is not a reaction.

apps.academic: A character's reaction shows how an event changes what he or she feels.
apps.spoken: What was your reaction when you saw it?
apps.writing: Use reaction to show how a character responds to an event.

cloze.s: Her ___ to the good news was to jump up and cheer.

cloze2.s: The class's ___ to the scary story was to gasp and then laugh nervously.

misuse.s: His reaction came three weeks before anything had happened.
misuse.why: A reaction follows an event; it cannot come before anything happens.

visual.alt: A surprised face with a flash beside it.

words.def: A hard effort to do something or to overcome a problem.
words.ex: The climber's struggle up the cliff took all day.
words.ex2: Learning to read in a new language can be a struggle.
words.nonExample: A job done easily and quickly is not a struggle.

apps.academic: In many stories, the main character's struggle leads to growth.
apps.spoken: It was a struggle to wake up this morning.
apps.writing: Use struggle for hard effort against a problem.

cloze.s: After a long ___ with the jammed door, Kim finally pushed it open.

cloze2.s: The hero's ___ against the strong river current took every bit of his strength.

misuse.s: Winning the game was an easy struggle that took no effort at all.
misuse.why: A struggle is hard effort; something that takes no effort is not a struggle.

visual.alt: A climber working hard to pull up a steep wall.

words.def: The way you think and feel about something, shown in your actions.
words.ex: Jo's positive attitude made the hard test seem easier.
words.ex2: The coach praised the team's helpful attitude after the game.
words.nonExample: The weather today is not an attitude.

apps.academic: A character's attitude toward a problem can change the whole story.
apps.spoken: She has a great attitude about learning.
apps.writing: Use attitude for a character's way of thinking and acting toward something.

cloze.s: Dan's cheerful ___ made everyone smile, even when the bus was late.

cloze2.s: Her curious ___ toward new subjects helped her learn faster.

misuse.s: Her attitude was a sandwich that she put in her lunch box.
misuse.why: An attitude is a way of thinking and feeling, not a food.

visual.alt: A smiling face with a star.

words.def: The way a story or problem ends, when the trouble is solved.
words.ex: In the resolution, the lost puppy was finally found.
words.ex2: The resolution of the argument came when both neighbors agreed to share the fence.
words.nonExample: The first page that introduces the characters is not the resolution.

apps.academic: In the resolution of a plot, the main conflict is settled.
apps.spoken: The resolution was happy, and everyone cheered.
apps.writing: Use resolution for the part of a story where the problem is solved.

cloze.s: In the ___ of the story, the lost puppy was returned to its owner.

cloze2.s: The ___ of the dispute came when both neighbors agreed to share the fence.

misuse.s: The resolution is the first page of the story, before any problem has happened.
misuse.why: The resolution comes when the problem is solved; the first page comes before the problem.

visual.alt: A check mark beside an open book.

words.def: To make something known that was secret or hidden.
words.ex: The detective will disclose the thief's name at the end of the story.
words.ex2: The museum refused to disclose where the painting had been hidden.
words.nonExample: Keeping a secret locked away is not disclosing it.

apps.academic: Authors disclose important facts at the right moment to surprise the reader.
apps.spoken: I can't disclose the secret yet.
apps.writing: Use disclose for making a secret known.

cloze.s: The mayor will ___ the winner's name at the end of the show.

cloze2.s: The author waits until the last chapter to ___ who sent the mysterious letter.

misuse.s: He disclosed the secret by never telling anyone and keeping it hidden forever.
misuse.why: To disclose is to make a secret known; keeping it hidden is the opposite.

passage.title: Book Talk: "The Storm Shutters"
paras: Ms. Lee's class was discussing a story called "The Storm Shutters." "Let's begin with the narrator," she said. "Who is telling this story?"
"Eli tells it himself," said Tariq. "Because he says I, we only know what Eli sees and feels."
"What is the main conflict?" asked Ms. Lee. Ana answered, "Eli wants to close the heavy shutters before a storm, but his father is away. Eli has to struggle with the boards alone."

"The author builds suspense," Tariq added. "We keep wondering if Eli will finish in time. Then there is a flashback to the day his father taught him to use a hammer, so we understand why Eli does not give up."
"Look at Eli's reaction when the first board slips," said Ana. "He takes a deep breath instead of crying. His attitude stays calm, and that is a trait we can see in his actions."

"What about the resolution?" Ms. Lee asked. "The shutters are closed just as the rain starts," Tariq said. "Then the last page will disclose that Eli's father was safe at a neighbor's house all along."
Ms. Lee smiled. "You have named every tool the author used."

qs.why: Eli has to move heavy boards alone, so struggle means a hard effort.

qs.q: What does the flashback to Eli's father help readers understand?
choices: Why Eli does not give up when the work is hard
Why the shutters were painted blue
qs.why: The flashback shows his father teaching him to use a hammer, which explains his confidence.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Lee smile at the end of the talk?
choices: The students named the story tools the author used.
She did not like the story.
She wanted to read the last page herself.
qs.why: She says they named every tool the author used, so she is pleased.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Eli has a calm attitude?
choices: The storm starts at the end.
He takes a deep breath instead of crying when the board slips.
qs.why: Taking a deep breath instead of crying shows calm.

qs.q: What is the passage mostly about?
choices: How to build storm shutters with a hammer
Why the narrator tells the story alone
A father who stays at a neighbor's house
How students use story words to explain how a story is built
qs.why: The students use words such as conflict and resolution to explain how the story works.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten literary words, read a book discussion between a teacher and students, practice the prefixes re- and dis- and the ending -ful, and write about plot, character, and narrator.

notes.va.flashback.n: A flashback shows an earlier time. Use a timeline: the story moves forward, and a flashback jumps back. Contrast with a dream or a memory told in one line.
notes.va.conflict.n: Conflict is a problem a character faces. It can be with another character, with nature, or inside a character. Ask: what is the problem?
notes.va.narrator.n: Narrator is the voice telling the story, which is not always a character. Show I versus he or she as clues.
notes.va.trait.n: A trait is a quality shown by actions. Students sometimes list feelings (sad); push for lasting qualities (brave, kind).
notes.va.suspense.n: Suspense is the feeling of wanting to know what will happen. Discuss which details add suspense: silence, ticking, a closed door.
notes.va.reaction.n: Reaction is how a character feels or acts in response. Show re- + action: a thing done back to an event.
notes.va.struggle.n: Teach struggle as a noun for a hard effort; students also hear it as a verb. Relate to conflict: struggle is how a character meets it.
notes.va.attitude.n: Attitude is how a person thinks and feels about something and shows it. Ask: what does the character's face and voice show?
notes.va.resolution.n: Resolution is when the problem is solved. In everyday use, resolution can also mean a decision (a New Year's resolution); mention the other sense only briefly.
notes.va.disclose.v: Disclose means to make a secret known. Compare it with tell: disclose usually involves something hidden.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'In the book talk, Tariq says there is a flashback to the day Eli's father taught him to use a hammer. A flashback goes back in time, and it explains why Eli does not give up. I can describe a flashback in my own story: a scene that shows how a character learned a skill.'

misconceptions: A narrator is always a character in the story.
A flashback is a character's dream.
Suspense is the same as fear.

Rewrite a paragraph from the narrator's point of view of another character.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit conflict and resolution as a pair two days later, again at one week, and reuse ambitious, selfish, and as a result when students explain what a character does and why.

wida.oral: Partner A tells one sentence of a familiar story. Partner B names the story part (conflict, suspense, flashback, resolution) and says why.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (escena retrospectiva, desenlace, rasgo, suspenso, revelar) not reviewed by a native speaker; flashback is often left in English in Spanish classrooms.
Resolution is taught only in the story sense; the sense of a decision or a screen setting is left for later.
The story "The Storm Shutters" is invented for this unit; no published text is quoted.
